claims.text: Redis Cluster splits the key space into 16384 slots, and a key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16384.
Each master node handles a subset of the 16384 hash slots.
Hash tags are a way to ensure that multiple keys are allocated in the same hash slot, which is what makes multi-key operations possible.
There are no proxies. A node that receives a query for a slot it does not serve looks up which node does and replies to the client with a MOVED error.
Nodes can be added and removed while the cluster is running. Both are the same operation: moving a hash slot from one node to another.

sections.heading: Replication and what can be lost

claims.text: Redis Cluster uses asynchronous replication between nodes, so there is always a window of time in which it is possible to lose writes during partitions.
A write may reach a master and be acknowledged to the client without having been propagated to its replicas; if the master then dies, the write is lost.
When a master fails, its replicas can start an election; only one wins and promotes itself to master, with the other masters voting.
The cluster survives partitions in which the majority of master nodes are reachable and there is at least one reachable replica for every master that is no longer reachable.

recall.prompt: How does Redis Cluster compute which slot a key belongs to?
A client sends a command to a node that does not serve the key's slot. What happens?

answer.text: The node does not proxy the request; it replies with a MOVED error pointing at the node that serves the slot.

recall.prompt: Why can Redis Cluster lose a write it has acknowledged?

answer.text: Replication is asynchronous, so a master can reply to the client and die before the write reaches its replicas.

recall.prompt: How is a node added to a running Redis Cluster?

answer.text: By moving hash slots to it from other nodes, while the cluster keeps running.
